159	  Acceptance Examples, Success Criteria, Scope Boundaries, Dependencies,
160	  Outstanding Questions, and Sources. This replaces the separate requirements
161	  artifact in new brainstorm-to-plan flows.
162	- **Planning Contract** — the implementation-facing decisions: Key Technical
163	  Decisions, high-level design, assumptions, implementation constraints,
164	  sequencing, and research that shapes how the Product Contract will be built.
165	- **Implementation Units** (with stable U-IDs) — discrete work packets sized so
166	  each is independently executable. Each unit names Goal, Requirements,
167	  Files, Approach, Test Scenarios, and Verification. `ce-work` and goal-mode
168	  executors consume these units.
169	  - **Unit Index (large plans only, ~10+ units).** When the plan has roughly
170	    ten or more units, open the section with a compact navigation table — one
171	    row per unit: **U-ID · one-line title · files touched · depends-on**. It
172	    lets an executor map units to files and resolve dependency order without
173	    scanning every unit body. It is a **navigation aid only**: the unit bodies
174	    stay authoritative, it carries nothing beyond those four fields (no
175	    approach, tests, or rationale), and `files touched` is the key/primary
176	    paths, not an exhaustive restatement. **Omit it below ~10 units** — there
177	    the per-unit `Dependencies`/`Files` (and any sequencing or dependency
178	    diagram) already suffice, and an index would be ceremony.
179	- **Verification Contract** — repo-specific commands and quality gates,
180	  including which tests prove the plan, when `release:validate` applies, and
181	  what behavioral skill evaluation is required. Avoid generic "run tests"
182	  language when the repo has concrete commands. When the goal is
183	  optimization-shaped (build time, latency, coverage, bundle size), express a
184	  measurable threshold as the exit criterion (e.g., "p95 latency < 200ms",
185	  "build time reduced 30%") and consider routing to `ce-optimize` — a metric
186	  target is a sharper done signal for a long-running goal than a boolean check.
187	- **Definition of Done** — global and per-unit done criteria. This is the
188	  completion contract for `/goal` or equivalent long-running workflows. Include
189	  a cleanup criterion: a long autonomous run accumulates dead-end and
190	  experimental code from approaches that did not pan out; declaring done
191	  requires that abandoned-attempt code is removed, not left in the diff.
192	
193	## Include when material
194	
195	These sections are present when they carry information that isn't covered
196	elsewhere. The test is not "is this a substantial plan?" — it is
197	*"does this specific plan have content this section would surface?"* Filling
198	a section with placeholder prose is worse than omitting it.
199	
200	The first five entries below carry the Product Contract's product framing —
201	what is being built and why. Later entries mix Product Contract subsections
202	(Scope Boundaries, Open Questions, Acceptance Examples, Sources) with
203	Planning Contract ones; the hard floor above remains authoritative for which
204	section sits under which contract. Problem Frame is unconditional; the other four fire on their own tests. A plan
205	that skips all four conditional framing entries has usually inherited its
206	framing from an upstream Product Contract — check before concluding none of
207	them fire.
208	
209	- **Problem Frame** — the hard floor above contains it unconditionally, so
210	  this entry governs its depth, never whether to include it. Give it
211	  paragraphs when motivation isn't obvious from Summary alone; keep it to a
212	  line or two when the motivation was settled upstream and more would only
213	  echo the origin document. Backward-looking / situational. Does NOT restate
214	  the proposal; the remedy lives in Summary.
215	
216	- **Key Decisions** — include when the plan carries product-level choices
217	  that constrain the Requirements below, whether made during planning (scope
218	  narrowings, defaults chosen against a real alternative, framing the user
219	  picked) or inherited from an upstream Product Contract, which Phase 0.3
220	  requires carrying forward with its rationale. Each entry is a provenance
221	  index entry, not a second statement of the rule: the decision in bold, at
222	  most one line of rationale, and exact `Governs R5, R7` links when it
223	  constrains specific requirements. The normative text lives on the governed
224	  Rs. Session-settled annotations follow the rules under "ID and content
225	  rules" below. Distinct from Planning Contract's Key Technical Decisions,
226	  which record how-level choices; a product decision belongs here, and a KTD
227	  cites it rather than mirroring it. Skip only when no such
228	  choice exists on any side: every requirement follows directly from the
229	  request, any upstream Product Contract weighed no alternatives, and the
230	  session settled none. A `session-settled:` decision always keeps the
231	  section — plan-write and the routing table both require its labeled entry
232	  to live here.
233	
234	- **Success Criteria** — include when there are quality / metric / handoff
235	  signals that Requirements don't already carry: quantitative metrics ("p95
236	  latency under 200ms"), qualitative criteria ("the agent's output reads as
237	  one voice"), process / handoff quality ("ce-doc-review can act on this
238	  without follow-ups"). Skip when Requirements ARE the success criteria
239	  (every R is "done when the R is true"). Requirements that describe an
240	  approach rather than an outcome are not success criteria; then include at
241	  least one criterion that would show the Goal Capsule Objective was reached.
242	
243	- **Actors** — include when the work has multi-party behavior (multiple
244	  humans, agents, or systems meaningfully involved) that the units must
245	  honor. Skip for single-actor work and for plans whose change is internal
246	  to one component — most implementation plans skip this.
247	
248	- **Key Flows** — include when the work has multi-step behavior whose
249	  sequencing the units must preserve. Skip when the change is not
250	  flow-shaped, or when Requirements and Acceptance Examples together already
251	  prevent downstream invention of paths — again, most implementation plans
252	  skip this.
253	
254	- **High-Level Technical Design** — include when the technical approach has
255	  shape that prose alone doesn't carry well: architecture across components,
256	  sequencing across processes, state machines, branching gates.
257	  Visualizations (component topology, sequence, swim lane, flowchart,
258	  data-flow) typically live here. Skip when the approach is a one-paragraph
259	  pattern application that the prose itself conveys.
260	
261	- **Scope Boundaries** — include when scope is contested, when there are
262	  tempting non-goals worth naming explicitly, or when "deferred for later"
263	  needs distinguishing from "outside the product's identity." Skip when scope
264	  is obvious from Requirements alone.
265	
266	- **Open Questions** — include when there are genuinely unresolved items that
267	  block planning or implementation. Skip when the plan is complete; an empty
268	  "Open Questions: none" section signals false uncertainty.
269	
270	- **System-Wide Impact** — include when the change affects cross-cutting
271	  concerns (data lifecycles, auth boundaries, performance posture, cardinal
272	  rules, shared infrastructure, agent/tool parity, prompt context, shared
273	  workspaces). Skip for changes localized to one component where the impact is
274	  self-evident.
275	
276	- **Risks & Dependencies** — include when there are real risks worth flagging
277	  (external service changes, version pins under churn, behavioral assumptions
278	  worth highlighting) or material upstream dependencies. Skip for low-risk
279	  localized work.
280	
281	- **Acceptance Examples** — include when any requirement has a state-dependent
282	  or conditional shape ("When X, Y") where the prose alone leaves ambiguity
283	  about edge cases. Skip when all requirements are unconditional and
284	  unambiguous.
285	
286	- **Documentation / Operational Notes** — include when documentation,
287	  monitoring, runbooks, or rollout steps need explicit notes. Skip when the
288	  work is purely internal and uses existing operational scaffolding without
289	  modification.
290	
291	- **Sources / Research** — surface the research that orients the implementer
292	  or justifies load-bearing choices. The test: *"if I were the implementer
293	  reading this cold, would this breadcrumb help me make better choices?"*
294	  Yes → surface (code locations like `services/convex/reports.ts:174-176`,
295	  external docs, RFCs, constraints, prior plans — the category is inclusive,
296	  not enumerated). Process exhaust (reading the user's prompt, glancing at
297	  obvious entry points, restating prose) → omit. Surface inline next to the
298	  KTD or unit it justifies, or as a dedicated section — both shapes work.
299	
300	## Agent agency
301	
302	The catalog is a floor, not a ceiling. When the plan's content doesn't fit
303	any catalog section, introduce a new one — don't force the content into a
304	section it doesn't belong in. Content drives section choices, not vice
305	versa.
306	
307	The agent also picks per artifact:
308	
309	- Whether Problem Frame merges into Summary — legacy and non-unified plans
310	  only. Any `ce-unified-plan/v1` artifact keeps both headings regardless of
311	  plan depth: the hard floor names them separately and downstream consumers
312	  anchor on them. (Scoped by artifact contract, not by depth — a `Lightweight`
313	  plan can still be implementation-ready.)
314	- Sub-groupings (Requirements by capability, KTDs by component, Units phased
315	  into milestones)
316	- How much detail each section carries
317	- Whether HTD has one diagram, several, or none — and whether visualizations
318	  live in HTD or embedded in other sections
319	
320	## Prose economy
321	
322	"Include when material" sizes *which* sections appear; this sizes *how the kept
323	prose reads*. A section can be material and still be written loosely — the
324	failure mode is a material section padded into a wall of text where
325	contradictions hide and the implementing agent loses the thread. A deep plan
326	earns length through coverage (more units, more traced requirements, real
327	risks), never through wordiness around that coverage.
328	
329	Hold every kept section to these:
330	
331	- **Lead with the decision or outcome.** Put the conclusion first, then the
332	  reason, then background; keep one claim plus its support per paragraph. Don't
333	  bury a Key Technical Decision, the chosen scope, an open blocker, or a unit
334	  goal beneath its rationale. This does not override section roles — Summary
335	  stays proposal-only, Problem Frame stays motivation-only and never restates
336	  the remedy.
337	- **Use an ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English (STE)-inspired style for
338	  technical plan content.** Write short, direct sentences. Keep one decision,
339	  action, or condition per sentence, and use one consistent term for each
340	  concept. Preserve exact identifiers, paths, commands, protocol names, and
341	  domain terms. Shorten sentences, not content: preserve every distinct
342	  requirement, qualification, and test scenario. A Summary is a handful of
343	  sentences, not one sentence with five semicolons and four parentheticals. A
344	  KTD's rationale is the load-bearing reason, not every reason.
345	- **A requirement or unit is one sentence of intent plus at most one
346	  qualifier.** When it would specify two outcomes ("either A or B, the
347	  implementer decides"), state the intent and send the fork to Open Questions —
348	  don't write both arms in full inside the item.
349	- **Cut hedges and intensifiers.** "Critically", "deliberately", "explicitly",
350	  "genuinely", "actually", "simply" carry nothing the implementer acts on.
351	- **Prefer the verb to the nominalization.** "Demote the grid", not "the
352	  demotion of the grid is the deliberate change in this plan".
353	
354	Precision is not padding: keep file paths, IDs, dates, domain terms,
355	conditionals, and exact thresholds verbatim; when a concrete anchor is knowable
356	from the work already done, use it instead of a vague abstraction. Economy
357	targets the connective tissue around precision, never the precision itself.
358	
359	**Resolve in place; don't stratify.** When deepening, a doc-review pass, or a
360	later decision supersedes earlier text, rewrite or remove the original — don't
361	leave it standing as strikethrough or stack a separate "resolutions" layer on
362	top of it. Version control holds the history. Stacked strata double the reading
363	surface and hide which text is live.
364	
365	**One owner per rule; cite, don't restate.** A normative rule — a gate, cap,
366	threshold, protocol, or output contract — is stated in full at exactly one
367	owning entry: product behavior on its R-ID; an implementation choice on its
368	KTD. Every other layer cites the owning ID and adds only what is local to
369	it — a unit's Approach carries unit-local deltas (files, sequencing,
370	patterns), never a re-derivation of the protocol its cited Rs and KTDs own.
371	Linked projections are sanctioned (an AE restating behavior under
372	`Covers R…`, a Flow citing the Rs it sequences). **Unlinked sibling
373	restatement** — the same rule written out again in a KTD, Scope bullet, or
374	Approach with no ID link — is the defect: each copy drifts independently.
375	When linked layers disagree, authority is typed: the **R wins on product
376	behavior**; the **KTD wins on implementation mechanism** within its cited R
377	constraints; a unit overrides neither; AEs and Flows illustrate and
378	sequence, never amend.
379	
380	**Bind external authorities; don't summarize them.** When a requirement,
381	KTD, or unit adopts an external document (a field guide, spec, standard),
382	state the commitment, cite the path, and record only this work's deltas. A
383	multi-sentence summary of the cited document is restatement of an owner that
384	lives outside the doc.
385	
386	**Named test, run before the plan is declared written:** could the implementer
387	find a contradiction in each section in one pass? Could a colleague who was
388	not in the session say what this work is after the Objective alone? A sentence
389	carrying more than one parenthetical, a sentence chaining more than two
390	semicolons, an item specifying two outcomes, or a rule stated in full in more than one section
391	fails the test — split it (a semicolon chain becomes a list), defer it, or
392	replace the duplicate with its owning ID.
393	
394	## Plan metadata fields
395	
396	Every plan carries a small set of stable metadata fields that downstream
397	tooling depends on. The contract is format-independent: in markdown these
398	fields appear as YAML frontmatter at the top of the file; in HTML they
399	appear as visible header text (typically a `<dl>` of `<dt>`/`<dd>` pairs or
400	a stats strip). Field names and semantics are the same across both formats
401	so consumers can locate them without knowing which format produced the
402	plan.
403	
404	### Required
405	
406	- **`title`** — the plan's descriptive name with a ` - Plan` suffix
407	  (e.g., `Highlighter Tool - Plan`), matching the H1 (markdown) or document
408	  `<h1>` (HTML) so file metadata and visible heading don't drift. Stable
409	  across readiness states (it is a plan at every stage). Do not put a
410	  conventional-commit prefix (`feat:`/`fix:`) in the title — the `type` field
411	  carries that classification.
412	- **`type`** — conventional-commit-prefix-aligned classification (`feat`,
413	  `fix`, `refactor`, `chore`, `docs`, `perf`, `test`, etc.). Carries the
414	  intent the eventual commit message should reflect.
415	- **`date`** — creation date in ISO 8601 (`YYYY-MM-DD`), ASCII digits only.
416	
417	Plans carry **no `status` field** — a plan is a decision artifact, not a
418	tracked work item. `ce-work` does not mutate the plan at ship time;
419	whether a plan shipped is derived from git, not stored in the doc. Do not
420	add a `status` field or an `active → completed` lifecycle.
421	
422	### Optional but well-known
423	
424	These fields are not required, but when set they have fixed names and
425	semantics so downstream tooling can rely on them:
426	
427	- **`origin`** — repo-relative path to an upstream brainstorm requirements
428	  doc (e.g., `docs/brainstorms/2026-05-12-pagination-requirements.md`).
429	  Set when planning from an upstream brainstorm; carried for traceability
430	  and re-resolved when `ce-plan` re-deepens.
431	- **`deepened`** — ISO 8601 date marking the first time the confidence
432	  check substantively strengthened the plan. Presence affects Phase 0.1
433	  resume fast-path logic (see `references/deepening-workflow.md`).
434	- **`execution`** — execution domain for downstream routing: `code`
435	  (the default when absent) or `knowledge-work`. `ce-work`'s input triage
436	  reads this: a plan marked `execution: knowledge-work` routes to the
437	  non-code carve-out (read sources, synthesize, produce a deliverable —
438	  skipping the branch/test/commit/CI lifecycle); absent or `code` routes
439	  to the normal code path. Written by `ce-plan`'s approach-altitude flow
440	  (`references/approach-altitude.md`) when a non-code deliverable is
441	  persisted for execution.
442	
443	Field names are stable across plan revisions — never rename a field or
444	repurpose its semantics. Agents composing new plans MUST use these exact
445	names; adding new fields is fine, but renaming `origin` to `source` or
446	`date` to `created` breaks the downstream consumers above.
447	
448	## ID and content rules
449	
450	These apply regardless of rendering format.
451	
452	- **Stable IDs.** R-IDs (Requirements), U-IDs (Implementation Units),
453	  KTD-IDs (Key Technical Decisions, implementation-ready plans), A-IDs
454	  (if Actors fire), F-IDs (if Flows fire), AE-IDs (if Acceptance Examples
455	  fire). IDs are stable across plan revisions — never renumber to "clean
456	  up gaps."
457	- **Plain prefix.** `R1.`, `U1.`, `KTD1.` as bullet prefixes. Do not bold;
458	  the prefix is visually distinctive on its own.
459	- **KTD-IDs on implementation-ready plans.** Number Key Technical Decisions
460	  (`KTD1.`, next unused number, same never-renumber rule as U-IDs) in newly
461	  authored implementation-ready plans, and in an existing plan whenever a
462	  KTD is added, split, or first cited by a unit. Untouched unnumbered KTDs
463	  in legacy plans stay as they are — readable by label, no mass renumbering.
464	- **Repo-relative paths.** Always. Never absolute paths in plan content;
465	  they break portability across machines, worktrees, teammates.
466	- **No process exhaust.** No "captured at Phase X" notes, no `## Next Steps`
467	  pointing to the next skill, no italic provenance lines. Engineering process
468	  metadata belongs in commit messages and tool output, not the artifact.
469	- **Session-settled annotations on KTDs.** A Key Technical Decision that
470	  records a decision settled in the invoking conversation carries an inline
471	  annotation on its entry:
472	  `(session-settled: user-directed — chosen over <alternative>: <one-line reason>)`.
473	  Exactly two classes: `user-directed` (the user chose against or between
474	  surfaced options) and `user-approved` (the agent proposed with the tradeoff
475	  surfaced; the user assented). An agent never labels its own unexamined
476	  proposal. A KTD that makes the how-level choice instantiating a labeled
477	  Product Contract Key Decision inherits the label and cites the decision's
478	  governed R-IDs. Do **not** create a KTD that merely mirrors a Product Key
479	  Decision with no new technical choice — the Key Decision plus its
480	  `Governs R…` links already own that content. The annotation is
481	  self-contained — decision, rejected alternative, and one-line reason
482	  readable without the conversation — and lives inline on the entry: no
483	  sidecar files, no frontmatter registry, no numeric weights, no lifecycle
484	  field. Like a `(see origin: <path>)` citation, it is decision provenance,
485	  not process exhaust — review passes must not strip it. A consumer that
486	  does not recognize the annotation treats the entry as a normal KTD.
487	- **Group Requirements by concern when they span distinct logical areas.**
488	  The trigger is distinct concerns, not item count — even four requirements
489	  benefit from grouping if they cover three different topics. Skip grouping
490	  only when all requirements are genuinely about the same thing; a long flat
491	  list is a smell that subgroups were missed. Group by capability (e.g.,
492	  "Packaging", "Migration and compatibility", "Contributor workflow"), not by
493	  the order requirements were discussed. R-IDs stay continuous across groups
494	  (R1, R2 in the first group; R3, R4 in the second; never restart at R1 per
495	  group).
496	
497	## Rendering
498	
499	The format-specific references describe how to render these sections in each
500	output format:
501	
502	- **Markdown rendering:** `references/markdown-rendering.md`
503	- **HTML rendering:** `references/html-rendering.md`
504	
505	This reference (`plan-sections.md`) is about WHAT the plan contains;
506	rendering references are about HOW each format presents it. The plan is
507	written in one format — markdown OR HTML, never both — based on the
508	resolved output mode. The section catalog is the same regardless of
509	format.
510

input.description: Read the spec-flow-analyzer prompt asset

result.output:
Analyze specifications, plans, and feature descriptions from the end user's perspective. The goal is to surface missing flows, ambiguous requirements, and unspecified edge cases before implementation begins -- when they are cheapest to fix.

## Phase 1: Ground in the Codebase

Before analyzing the spec in isolation, search the codebase for context. This prevents generic feedback and surfaces real constraints.

1. Use the native content-search tool (e.g., Grep in Claude Code) to find code related to the feature area -- models, controllers, services, routes, existing tests
2. Use the native file-search tool (e.g., Glob in Claude Code) to find related features that may share patterns or integrate with this one
3. Note existing patterns: how does the codebase handle similar flows today? What conventions exist for error handling, auth, validation?

This context shapes every subsequent phase. Gaps are only gaps if the codebase doesn't already handle them.

> **Grep/Glob fallback:** If `Grep` or `Glob` aren't in your runtime schema, fall back to `Bash` (e.g., `rg -li`, `find`) with the same patterns and case-insensitivity as Phase 1. Prefer the native tools when present.

## Phase 2: Map User Flows

Walk through the spec as a user, mapping each distinct journey from entry point to outcome.

For each flow, identify:
- **Entry point** -- how the user arrives (direct navigation, link, redirect, notification)
- **Decision points** -- where the flow branches based on user action or system state
- **Happy path** -- the intended journey when everything works
- **Terminal states** -- where the flow ends (success, error, cancellation, timeout)

Focus on flows that are actually described or implied by the spec. Don't invent flows the feature wouldn't have.

## Phase 3: Find What's Missing

Compare the mapped flows against what the spec actually specifies. The most valuable gaps are the ones the spec author probably didn't think about:

- **Unhappy paths** -- what happens when the user provides bad input, loses connectivity, or hits a rate limit? Error states are where most gaps hide.
- **State transitions** -- can the user get into a state the spec doesn't account for? (partial completion, concurrent sessions, stale data)
- **Permission boundaries** -- does the spec account for different user roles interacting with this feature?
- **Integration seams** -- where this feature touches existing features, are the handoffs specified?

Use what was found in Phase 1 to ground this analysis. If the codebase already handles a concern (e.g., there's global error handling middleware), don't flag it as a gap.

## Phase 4: Formulate Questions

For each gap, formulate a specific question. Vague questions ("what about errors?") waste the spec author's time. Good questions name the scenario and make the ambiguity concrete.

**Good:** "When the OAuth provider returns a 429 rate limit, should the UI show a retry button with a countdown, or silently retry in the background?"

**Bad:** "What about rate limiting?"

For each question, include:
- The question itself
- Why it matters (what breaks or degrades if left unspecified)
- A default assumption if it goes unanswered

## Output Format

### User Flows

Number each flow. Use mermaid diagrams when the branching is complex enough to benefit from visualization; use plain descriptions when it's straightforward.

### Gaps

Organize by severity, not by category:

1. **Critical** -- blocks implementation or creates security/data risks
2. **Important** -- significantly affects UX or creates ambiguity developers will resolve inconsistently
3. **Minor** -- has a reasonable default but worth confirming

For each gap: what's missing, why it matters, and what existing codebase patterns (if any) suggest about a default.

### Questions

Numbered list, ordered by priority. Each entry: the question, the stakes, and the default assumption.

### Recommended Next Steps

Concrete actions to resolve the gaps -- not generic advice. Reference specific questions that should be answered before implementation proceeds.

## Principles

- **Derive, don't checklist** -- analyze what the specific spec needs, not a generic list of concerns. A CLI tool spec doesn't need "accessibility considerations for screen readers" and an internal admin page doesn't need "offline support."
- **Ground in the codebase** -- reference existing patterns. "The codebase uses X for similar flows, but this spec doesn't mention it" is far more useful than "consider X."
- **Be specific** -- name the scenario, the user, the data state. Concrete examples make ambiguities obvious.
- **Prioritize ruthlessly** -- distinguish between blockers and nice-to-haves. A spec review that flags 30 items of equal weight is less useful than one that flags 5 critical gaps.

# Final Review and Plan Write

Phase 5.1 through 5.3.2 of `ce-plan`, on the Durable path only. Read this before writing the plan file.

### Phase 5: Final Review, Write File, and Handoff

#### 5.1 Review Before Writing

Before finalizing, check:
- The plan does not invent product behavior that should have been defined in `ce-brainstorm`
- If there was no origin document, the bounded planning bootstrap established enough product clarity to plan responsibly
- Every major decision is grounded in the origin document or research
- Each implementation unit is concrete, dependency-ordered, and implementation-ready
- If test-first proof, characterization coverage, smoke-first verification, or another execution direction was explicit or strongly implied, the relevant units carry it forward with a lightweight natural-language `Execution note`
- Each feature-bearing unit has test scenarios from every applicable category (happy path, edge cases, error paths, integration) — right-sized to the unit's complexity, not padded or skimped
- Test scenarios name specific inputs, actions, and expected outcomes without becoming test code
- Feature-bearing units with blank or missing test scenarios are flagged as incomplete — feature-bearing units must have actual test scenarios, not just an annotation. The `Test expectation: none -- [reason]` annotation is only valid for non-feature-bearing units (pure config, scaffolding, styling)
- Deferred items are explicit and not hidden as fake certainty
- Every implementation unit that implements a session-settled decision cites its settled owner in Requirements or Approach: the labeled KTD by `KTD<N>` for a planning decision, or the governing R-IDs for a product decision whose labeled Key Decision `Governs` them. The cited excerpt — the KTD directly, or the Key Decision reverse-resolved through its `Governs R…` links — is the channel through which executors receive the label
- Every meaning-preserving R split or ownership move re-points affected `Governs R…`, `Covers R…`, and inline `per R…` citations to the resulting owning IDs; no pre-restructure catch-all link silently excludes a split-out requirement
- **High-Level Technical Design presence audit (load-bearing).** For each architecture trigger in Phase 3.4 that the plan content satisfies (3+ components with directed relationships, 3+ protocol steps, 3+ state machine states, lifecycle, 3+ decision points, 3+ data-flow stages, mode/flag combinations, DSL/API surface design, non-obvious single-component shape), verify a corresponding sketch/diagram is present in the High-Level Technical Design section. Count the firing triggers; count the sketches; the sketch count must be at least the count of distinct trigger categories that fired. Missing the section when a trigger fired, OR including the section but skipping a triggered sketch within it, is incomplete — return to Phase 3.4 and add the missing sketch. Token cost is not a valid reason to fail this check.
- If a High-Level Technical Design section is included, it uses the right medium for the work, carries the non-prescriptive framing, and does not contain implementation code (no imports, exact signatures, or framework-specific syntax)
- Per-unit technical design fields, if present, are concise and directional rather than copy-paste-ready
- If the plan creates a new directory structure, would an Output Structure tree help reviewers see the overall shape?
- If Scope Boundaries lists items that are planned work for a separate PR, issue, or repo, are they under `### Deferred to Follow-Up Work` rather than mixed with true non-goals?
- U-IDs are unique within the plan and follow the stability rule — no two units share an ID; reordering or splitting did not renumber existing units; gaps from deletions are preserved
- Would a visual aid (dependency graph, interaction diagram, comparison table) help a reader grasp the plan structure faster than scanning prose alone?

If the plan originated from a requirements document, re-read that document and verify:
- The chosen approach still matches the product intent
- Scope boundaries and success criteria are preserved
- Blocking questions were either resolved, explicitly assumed, or sent back to `ce-brainstorm`
- Every section of the origin document is addressed in the plan — scan each section to confirm nothing was silently dropped
- If origin supplies A/F/AE IDs: every origin R/F/AE that *affects implementation* is referenced in Requirements, a U-ID unit, test scenarios, verification, scope boundaries, or explicitly deferred. Actors are carried forward when they affect behavior, permissions, UX, orchestration, handoff, or verification. The standard is preservation of product intent, not mandatory ID spam — irrelevant origin IDs may be omitted
- If origin was Deep-product (origin contains an `Outside this product's identity` subsection): the plan's Scope Boundaries preserves the three-way split — `Deferred for later` and `Outside this product's identity` carried verbatim from origin, `Deferred to Follow-Up Work` reserved for plan-local implementation sequencing

#### 5.1.5 Brainstorm-Sourced Scoping Synthesis

Surface plan-time call-outs to the user before Phase 5.2 commits the plan to disk — the latest cheap moment to catch plan-time scope errors. The brainstorm already validated WHAT to build; this phase surfaces HOW the plan will execute on the forks that matter.

Fires **whenever Phase 0.2 resolved an upstream Product Contract source** — a requirements-only unified plan (an explicit path, or a discovered `product_contract_source: ce-brainstorm` plan in `<root>/plans/`) **or** a legacy `*-requirements.{md,html}` brainstorm doc — AND not on Phase 0.1 fast paths (resume normal, deepen-intent). The new `ce-brainstorm` -> `ce-plan <unified-plan>` enrichment flow is brainstorm-sourced and MUST fire this gate, just like legacy flows. Skip Phase 5.1.5 only in solo invocation (no upstream source found; `product_contract_source: ce-plan-bootstrap`) — solo plans handled their synthesis in Phase 0.7.

**Read `references/synthesis-summary.md` before composing the scoping synthesis.** It carries the affirmability test, keep-test criteria, detail test, summary shape budgets, the literal confirmation and auto-proceed templates, granularity rules, anti-patterns, revision-vs-confirmation discipline, doc-body reading rules, doc-shape routing, soft-cut behavior, self-redirect support, the worked PII compression example, and full headless-mode routing — all required for a well-shaped synthesis.

**Required gate output — do not skip; silent proceeding is not allowed.** Compose an internal three-bucket scope draft (Stated / Inferred / Out of scope — internal thinking that feeds plan-body routing at Phase 5.2, not the chat output). Derive call-outs (specific forks where user input materially changes the plan), run the pre-emit scans, then emit the **brainstorm-sourced** synthesis and **wait for user confirmation before continuing to Phase 5.2.** Its summary is two parts — a 1-2 sentence restatement of the brainstorm's scope in the brainstorm's own vocabulary, then the plan-specific scoping decisions the brainstorm did not make (full-brainstorm coverage vs. narrowed subset; adjacent refactors in or out; test scope at scenario level) — each affirmable without reading code, and never an enumeration of Implementation Units, file paths, or PR/sequencing shape. Emit the confirmation or auto-proceed template as specified in `references/synthesis-summary.md` (loaded above) rather than reconstructing it here.

**Blocking decision:** auto-proceed — announce without waiting — only when plan depth is **Lightweight AND zero call-outs survive**. Standard and Deep always fire the confirmation gate, even with zero call-outs.

**Headless / opt-in skip:** in headless mode, or when `SKIP_SCOPING_CONFIRM` resolved to skip in Phase 0.0, do not block — compose the internal draft, skip the chat-time confirmation, and route Inferred bets to a `## Assumptions` section at plan-write (Phase 5.2). The skip covers only this scoping confirmation; Phase 0.4 routing, Phase 0.5 blockers, Phase 2 questions, source-doc disambiguation, and the Phase 5.4 menu still fire. Announcement wording and full routing: `references/synthesis-summary.md` ("Headless mode", "When to skip the blocking confirmation").

#### 5.2 Write Plan File

Return to the kernel for its model-elevation boundary. Resume here only after that step has settled; this reference does not dispatch the authoring route itself.

**REQUIRED: Write the plan file to disk before presenting any options.**

Both markdown and HTML plans continue through `ce-doc-review`; fixes apply in
the artifact's native format while preserving its existing structure.

Use the Write tool to save the complete plan to the resolved format's extension:

```text
<root>/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-HHMM-<type>-<descriptive-name>-plan.<md|html>
```

Extension follows `OUTPUT_FORMAT` from Phase 0.0 — `.md` when markdown, `.html` when HTML. The filename prefix is the local wall-clock time at write, so ordering comes from the clock rather than a daily counter. Reserve the final path atomically; when creating a new artifact, an exact-path collision retries with the smallest available numeric suffix rather than overwriting. Explicit format conversion is not a new artifact and is exempt from that suffix: it keeps the existing basename, changes only the extension, and writes that exact sibling path, updating it in place when it already exists. A suffixed conversion output would break the same-basename staleness signal Phase 0.2 and `ce-work` discovery depend on.

Compose the plan using the content from `references/plan-sections.md` and the format-specific principles from the rendering reference loaded at Phase 0.0 (`markdown-rendering.md` OR `html-rendering.md`).

**Write tight.** A section being material is not license to pad it. Hold every kept section to the prose-economy discipline in `references/plan-sections.md`: lead with the decision or outcome, one idea per sentence, a requirement or unit is intent plus at most one qualifier, defer forks to Open Questions rather than specifying both arms, resolve superseded text in place rather than stacking strata. Before declaring the plan written, run the named test there — could the implementer find a contradiction in each section in one pass?

Write the unified plan artifact according to `references/plan-sections.md`.

- If the source is a requirements-only unified plan, update that file in place unless `OUTPUT_FORMAT`, pipeline mode, or an explicit conversion requires a new canonical path. Preserve Product Contract meaning and stable IDs under Phase 0.3 step 3; sanctioned meaning-preserving restructuring remains allowed and carries its preservation-note and citation-repointing obligations. Add Planning Contract, Implementation Units, Verification Contract, and Definition of Done. When a new canonical path *is* required (format conversion), the original artifact is left in place but is **no longer canonical** — it keeps its `requirements-only` metadata, so discovery treats a requirements-only artifact that has an implementation-ready same-basename sibling as superseded (see Phase 0.2 step 2 and `ce-work`'s blank-invocation discovery) rather than re-enriching or stopping on it.
- If the source is a legacy requirements doc, create a new unified plan in `<root>/plans/` and carry the legacy path in `origin:`.
- If this is direct planning, create a complete unified plan in `<root>/plans/` with `product_contract_source: ce-plan-bootstrap`.
- Set `artifact_contract: ce-unified-plan/v1`, `artifact_readiness: implementation-ready`, and `execution: code` for software implementation plans.
- Do not set `artifact_contract: ce-unified-plan/v1` on universal-planning outputs, answer-seeking outputs, or approach-plans unless they include the full software implementation contract.
- Do not write a launch prompt into the doc. The launch prompt is generated at handoff (Phase 5.4 menu — `/goal` copy-paste on Claude Code, `create_goal` on Codex) from the plan's current content, so it never goes stale; it points to Goal Capsule, Verification Contract, Definition of Done, and U-IDs rather than duplicating them.

**Session-settled decisions at plan-write.** A settled *planning* decision (a how-level choice made this session) is authored as a numbered, labeled Key Technical Decision carrying the annotation `(session-settled: user-directed — chosen over <alternative>: <one-line reason>)` (class per `references/settled-decisions.md`: `user-directed` or `user-approved`). A settled *product* decision already lives on its Product Contract Key Decision with `Governs R…` links — do **not** mirror it into a KTD; a KTD that makes the how-level choice instantiating it inherits the label and cites the governed R-IDs.

**HTML composition timing.** When `OUTPUT_FORMAT=html`, Phase 5.3 deepening runs before this write completes its final form, then `ce-doc-review` applies any fixes directly in the HTML artifact's native structure. The artifact returned after Phase 5.3.8 reflects both deepening synthesis and document review.

Confirm (use absolute path so the reference is clickable in modern terminals):

```text
Plan written to <absolute path to plan>
```

**The pipeline-mode exception SKILL.md points here for:** when research produced invalidating evidence (infeasible, wrong-thing, destructive) against any session-settled decision in play for the run — whether carried in the caller brief or already carried as a `session-settled:` label in the artifact being enriched (brainstorm Key Decisions or plan KTDs) — do not write the plan and do not resolve silently — return a blocked report to the caller containing the token `settled-decision-invalidated`, the decision, and the reason, parallel to the non-software pipeline stop in `references/universal-planning.md`, so the caller can stop.

**CONCEPTS.md gap-fill (only if the file already exists):** If the plan body uses a domain term whose definition is missing from `CONCEPTS.md`, add the entry. **Domain entities, named processes, and status concepts with project-specific meaning only** — not file paths, class names, function signatures, or implementation decisions. `CONCEPTS.md` is a glossary, not a spec or catch-all. A term whose whole meaning an existing entry already carries is a refinement of that entry, not a new heading. Follow the format set by existing entries. Apply silently. Skip entirely if `CONCEPTS.md` does not exist — creation and folding are owned by ce-compound and ce-compound-refresh; retiring or deleting an entry is ce-compound-refresh's alone.

#### 5.3 Confidence Check and Deepening

A deepen run enters here from Phase 0.1 without passing intake. For a material Durable run, use the host's task-tracking capability when available to show route-level outcomes and meaningful transitions; if unavailable, continue without simulating it in chat.

Auto mode is the default during plan generation and synthesizes subagent findings directly into the plan. Interactive mode is activated by the Phase 0.1 re-deepen fast path and presents each finding for the user to accept or reject. Pipeline runs always use auto mode.

Interactive mode exists because on-demand deepening is a different user posture — the user already has a plan they are invested in and wants to be surgical about what changes. This applies whether the plan was generated by this skill, written by hand, or produced by another tool.

##### 5.3.1 Classify Plan Depth and Topic Risk

Determine the plan depth from the document:
- **Lightweight** - small, bounded, low ambiguity, usually 2-4 implementation units
- **Standard** - moderate complexity, some technical decisions, usually 3-6 units
- **Deep** - cross-cutting, high-risk, or strategically important work, usually 4-8 units or phased delivery

Build a risk profile. Treat these as high-risk signals:
- Authentication, authorization, or security-sensitive behavior
- Payments, billing, or financial flows
- Data migrations, backfills, or persistent data changes
- External APIs or third-party integrations
- Privacy, compliance, or user data handling
- Cross-interface parity or multi-surface behavior
- Significant rollout, monitoring, or operational concerns

##### 5.3.2 Gate: Decide Whether to Deepen

- **Lightweight** plans usually do not need deepening unless they are high-risk
- **Standard** plans often benefit when one or more important sections still look thin
- **Deep** or high-risk plans often benefit from a targeted second pass
- **Thin local grounding override:** If Phase 1.2 triggered external research because local patterns were thin (fewer than 3 direct examples or adjacent-domain match), always proceed to scoring regardless of how grounded the plan appears. When the plan was built on unfamiliar territory, claims about system behavior are more likely to be assumptions than verified facts. The scoring pass is cheap — if the plan is genuinely solid, scoring finds nothing and exits quickly
- **Load-bearing external research override:** If Phase 1.4 marked external research as load-bearing (it materially shaped a KTD, Alternative, Scope boundary, or Risk), always proceed to scoring — **even when local implementation patterns are strong**. A landscape or prior-art finding can shape recommendations the local codebase cannot verify, and the thin-grounding override above would miss it. This enters the scoring pass only; it does not force deepening

If the plan already appears sufficiently grounded and neither the thin-grounding nor the load-bearing-external-research override applies, report "Confidence check passed — no sections need strengthening", then **load `references/plan-handoff.md` now and execute 5.3.8 → 5.3.9 → 5.4 in sequence**. Document review is mandatory for both markdown and HTML plans — do not skip it because the confidence check passed. The two tools catch different classes of issues.

##### 5.3.3–5.3.7 Deepening Execution

When deepening is warranted, read `references/deepening-workflow.md` for confidence scoring checklists, section-to-agent dispatch mapping, execution mode selection, research execution, interactive finding review, and plan synthesis instructions. Execute steps 5.3.3 through 5.3.7 from that file, then hand control back to SKILL.md at 5.3.8. Deepening is not a terminal state — the run always continues to the handoff, and `deepening-workflow.md` owns which step it re-enters at, including its interactive no-accepted-findings path straight to 5.4.

## Stage 2: chat-time scoping synthesis

Stage 2 is what the user actually sees. The shape differs between variants because they serve different purposes — brainstorm-sourced plans inherit a validated WHAT and surface plan-specific HOW; solo plans have no upstream and the synthesis is the WHAT.

### Brainstorm-sourced shape (Phase 5.1.5)

Two content sections plus call-outs:

1. **Brainstorm-scope restatement** (1-2 sentences, prose). Restates the brainstorm's scope as orientation. The user wrote this content, but the synthesis may be read days later or in parallel with other plans — the restatement is the topic anchor that says "this is the artifact we're planning against." Stay in the brainstorm's own vocabulary. Do NOT enumerate Implementation Units, restate constraints back at the user, or list acceptance examples.

2. **Plan-specific scoping decisions** (prose, or bullets when multi-faceted). Scope-level commitments the agent made that the brainstorm did not: does this plan cover the full brainstorm scope or narrow to a subset; are adjacent refactors pulled in or held out; what test scope at scenario level (which sites, which acceptance examples). Each item must pass the **affirmability test** — the user can affirm or redirect it without reading code. This section is scope claims at affirm-or-redirect level, NOT a description of where the implementation reaches, NOT PR count or commit sequencing, NOT Implementation Unit lists, NOT exact file paths or test commands — those are all plan-write outputs the synthesis cannot honestly claim. If the plan covers the full brainstorm scope with no narrowing, expansions, or adjacent work, this section stays short ("This plan covers the full brainstorm scope; test scope is X").

3. **Call outs** (zero or more, capped by plan depth — see "How many call-outs are right?" below). Each a real fork where the user's input materially changes the plan. Omit the "Call outs:" header entirely when zero forks survived the keep test.

### Solo shape (Phase 0.7)

No upstream document; the synthesis itself is the scope claim:

1. **Scope claim** (prose, or bullets when multi-faceted). What the agent is planning to build, at affirm-or-redirect level — names what's in and what's out. NOT an enumeration of Implementation Units the plan will contain.

2. **Call outs** (zero or more, capped by plan depth). Same as brainstorm-sourced.

### Shape budgets

Tier-aware budgets are **ceilings, not targets**. Less is correct when there isn't more to say — filling the budget produces noise.

| Plan depth | Restatement (brainstorm-sourced) | Plan-specific scoping (brainstorm-sourced) / Scope claim (solo) |
|---|---|---|
| Lightweight | 1 sentence | 1-3 lines prose |
| Standard | 1-2 sentences | up to 3-5 lines or 2-4 bullets |
| Deep | 1-2 sentences | up to 4-6 lines or 3-6 bullets |

Form within each section (prose, bullets, mix) follows whatever communicates best.

### Shared rules

- **No "Stated" bucket in chat** (the orientation or scope-claim covers it).
- **No "Out of scope" bucket as a separate list** — fold a non-obvious exclusion into a call-out when it survives the keep test, otherwise drop it.
- **Session-settled decisions render as `Carrying forward:` lines, never call-outs.** One line each — decision, class, and what it was chosen over — placed before Call outs in both templates. The keep test excludes them from call-outs: a fork the user already closed is not a fork.
- **Source-document vocabulary.** When a brainstorm exists, use its terms. Don't invent agent-coded shorthand (e.g., "skill-instruction shape", "hooks engine selection at Step 2a entry"). When referencing acceptance examples, requirements, or flows, name them in plain terms ("the install-prompt acceptance case") — never use bare IDs.

- **Pre-emit mechanical checks.** Before emitting the synthesis, scan the output:
  - **Bare ID references** (`AE\d+`, `R\d+`, `F\d+`, `A\d+`, `U\d+`) → replace with plain names. Mixed forms (case named AND ID cited) still violate the rule because the ID adds noise without information.
  - **File paths** (`path/like.md`, `path/like.py`, `internal/cli/...`, `skills/.../...`, etc.) → cut unless the path IS the topic of an explicit fork in the call-outs. Allowed: "cleanup hook in the existing archive step vs. a new dedicated phase" (where the path is implicit in the decision). Forbidden: paths listed to demonstrate completeness, preview Implementation Units, or describe where the implementation reaches. The synthesis names *what* the plan targets, not *where* the code lives.

### The keep test for each call-out

Before keeping a candidate call-out from the internal draft, run the **affirmability test**: would the user need to look at code to evaluate this? If yes, it is plan-body content — cut. If no, apply the keep test — one of the following must be true:

- **Real fork**: another reasonable agent might choose differently on this dimension (extend pattern X vs. introduce abstraction Y; scan source A vs. source B; etc.)
- **Non-obvious behavioral choice**: a default the agent picked that the user would not see by reading the summary alone, but that materially affects what the plan does (e.g., "scans the working-dir snapshot before the copy step" — the user would not infer the scan target from a description of the gate's purpose)
- **Non-obvious exclusion**: an item was deliberately excluded that the user might want to add back in
- **Cheap-now-expensive-later correction**: a bet the user is well-placed to redirect now that would be expensive to undo after research or plan-write

Cut anything else, including:

- Mechanical items where there is no real alternative (e.g., "no new dependencies" when the work clearly does not need any)
- Implementation choices that will be settled during the work (e.g., regex precision tuned during impl)
- Items already implied by the summary

### The detail test (per call-out and per summary bullet)

After the keep test, every surviving item runs the **detail test**: 1-2 lines max, conversational not documentary. A call-out or summary bullet that runs to 4+ lines of dense prose is naming an implementation consequence rather than a decision — re-cut at higher abstraction.

The keep test addresses *which* items survive. The detail test addresses *how much* each surviving item says. Without it, the count cap is gameable: an agent can hit "3 call-outs" while each call-out is a 6-line paragraph, and the synthesis reads as a doc preview instead of a checkpoint.

### How many call-outs are right?

The cap is heuristic, not law. The real discipline is the keep test on each candidate. Typical bounds by plan depth:

| Plan depth | Typical | Cap |
|---|---|---|
| Lightweight | 0-2 | 3 |
| Standard | 1-3 | 4 |
| Deep | 2-5 | 6 |

**If the stage-2 pass exceeds the tier cap, OR any call-out or summary bullet runs to 4+ lines of dense prose, the synthesis is misshapen — do not raise the cap or accept the bloat, re-cut at a higher level of abstraction.** Almost always, 2-3 of those call-outs are sub-decisions of one larger fork (file path, flag name, JSON key behavior, and dependency choice are usually four facets of one "how to extend the existing scaffold" decision, not four independent forks). Collapse related call-outs into a single decision named at the level the user actually weighs in on. The user's job is to redirect forks, not to validate every implementation consequence of a fork they have already implicitly agreed to by accepting the higher-level decision.

A useful test: read the call-outs aloud. If two or more sound like "and also" extensions of the same idea, they belong as one.

### Anti-patterns in call-outs

Each anti-pattern below produces a call-out that fails the affirmability test. If a candidate call-out matches one of these, it is plan-body content — cut, do not rephrase.

- Names a file path or module name (`internal/artifacts/pii.go`)
- Names a flag, env var, or exact env value (`--accept-redaction-list=<finding-id,...>`)
- Specifies a JSON shape, response format, or exact data structure
- Names HTTP status codes, event names, or exact error wording
- Describes implementation flow ("first X, then Y, then Z")
- Names exact method signatures, call graphs, or SQL syntax
- States a mechanical choice with no real alternative ("uses stdlib regexp")

The line-number, signature, and code-spec rules are not new — they have always been forbidden in Inferred bullets. They apply equally to call-outs, which are now the user-facing surface.

---

## When to skip the blocking confirmation

The auto-proceed path (announce without waiting for user confirmation) fires only when **plan depth is Lightweight AND zero call-outs survive the keep test**. For Standard or Deep plans, always fire the confirmation gate even when zero call-outs survive — substance earns the checkpoint, not interaction history. A Deep plan with rich silent decisions and a 1-3 line summary is exactly the case where rubber-stamping is most likely; the explicit confirmation request gives the user a real chance to push back before research or plan-write proceeds.
## Brainstorm-sourced variant (Phase 5.1.5)

Fires only when:
- Phase 0.2 found upstream brainstorm doc (brainstorm-sourced invocation)
- AND not on Phase 0.1 fast paths

**Content focus**: plan-time decisions only. The brainstorm + R1 synthesis already validated WHAT to build; the internal draft and stage 2 surface HOW the plan will execute that work — decisions the brainstorm did not make.

Items to surface in the internal draft:
- **Files/modules to touch (and not touch)** — what the implementation reaches into
- **Patterns extended vs. introduced new** — architectural decisions the agent made within confirmed scope (R2's content focus, not bias toward either direction)
- **Test scope** — which existing-but-untested code is in/out of test scope for this work
- **Refactor scope** — adjacent cleanup, if any, going to deferred items vs. active diff
- **Cross-cutting impact** — auth, migrations, shared types when they're touched

Most of these will not survive the keep test as separate call-outs. Surface only the forks where another reasonable agent might choose differently and the user can correct cheaply now.

**Reads from the Product Contract, not a synthesis section**: the upstream artifact is a requirements-only unified plan (`product_contract_source: ce-brainstorm`), not a separate brainstorm doc, and it has no `## Synthesis` section (the synthesis is a chat-time artifact in ce-brainstorm; only the prose summary embeds, under the Product Contract). Phase 5.1.5 derives plan-time decisions from the Product Contract's sections — Summary, Problem Frame, Requirements, Key Flows, Scope Boundaries — plus Phase 1 research. Legacy standalone requirements docs (`origin: docs/brainstorms/...`) and older brainstorms that may carry a legacy `## Synthesis` section still work; that content is treated as supplementary, not authoritative, with the Product Contract / body sections taking precedence.

**Why pre-write, not pre-research**: brainstorm doc + R1 synthesis already validated WHAT, so research is well-targeted. Plan-time decisions emerge during research and structuring (Phases 1-4), so pre-write catches them at the latest cheap moment — before Phase 5.2 commits the plan to disk.

### Stage 2 template (brainstorm-sourced)

**Summary discipline (required):** describe **how the implementation approaches the work** at a high level — files/modules touched, patterns extended vs. introduced, scope boundaries the plan honors. Forward-looking (what *will* be in the plan), not retrospective. Brainstorm-validated WHAT is assumed; the summary covers HOW. Form (prose, bullets, mix) and length follow the tier budget in "Stage 2: chat-time scoping synthesis" above; detail test applies per bullet.

**Anti-fluff guidance:** lead with the actual implementation shape in plain words. No qualifiers, no re-stating the brainstorm's WHAT. If the summary just restates the brainstorm's Problem Frame, rewrite it to focus on plan-time decisions.

**Confirmation template (fires for Standard/Deep regardless of call-out count, or for any tier with one or more call-outs surviving):**

```
The brainstorm scopes [1-2 sentence restatement of the brainstorm's scope as orientation; in the brainstorm's own vocabulary; NOT an enumeration of Implementation Units, constraints, or acceptance examples].

This plan [plan-specific scoping: what's covered vs. deferred vs. expanded relative to the brainstorm; test scope; any adjacent refactors pulled in or held out. Prose or bullets per substance].

**Carrying forward:** (omit this header when no session-settled decisions exist)
- [settled decision in 1 line: decision — class; chosen over <alternative>]

**Call outs:** (omit this header when zero forks survived the keep test)
- [plan-time fork in 1-2 lines: name the choice and optional one-clause trade-off in parens. NO multi-sentence rationale, NO "my default is X" pitch — those belong in Key Technical Decisions in the plan body, not the synthesis]

Confirm and I'll write the plan next, drawing on the brainstorm, research, and this synthesis.
```

**Auto-proceed template (fires only for Lightweight with zero call-outs):**

```
Planning [brief brainstorm-scope restatement] — [plan-specific shape in one clause].

No open decisions to weigh in on — proceeding to plan-write. Interrupt if I have the scope wrong.
```

Then continue to Phase 5.2 without waiting. Use prose for any user response that does arrive. Justification is Interaction Rule 5(a).

---

## Soft-cut on circularity (shared)

Track which call-outs the user touched per round. The soft-cut blocking question fires **only when the same call-out is revised twice** (or a third-round revision targets a call-out already revised in round two). New-call-out revisions across rounds proceed without limit.

## 学びの検索結果

### 検索コンテキスト
- **対象作業**: `review-triage` プラグインの実装計画の肉付け。`recurrence-detection.md` と `reframing.md` の削除、周回数の閾値 N によるプランナー選択の導入、`review-triage-fix` の 3 段階 (調査/立案/修正) へのサブエージェント化、`loop.max_rounds` の既定値変更
- **使用したキーワード**: review-triage, 正本, 記録 YAML, エージェント入力, サブエージェント, 実効モデル, effort, relative-path, agent-input
- **走査したファイル数**: 6 件（`docs/solutions/` 全件）
- **関連度の高い一致**: 4 件（うち 1 件は module が review-triage 本体）

### 関連する学び

#### 1. 検査ツールの相対パスは基準を推測せず明示させる
- **ファイル**: `docs/solutions/tooling-decisions/require-explicit-basis-for-relative-paths.md`（2026-09-02）
- **モジュール**: review-triage（`triagecheck` 本体）
- **Problem Type**: `tooling_decision`
- **関連性**: 今回の計画が対象とする `review-triage` プラグイン自身の学び。ループの状態機械を作り直し、`review-triage-fix` の各段をサブエージェントで走らせる構成に変えると、プロセスのカレントディレクトリと記録の置き場 (`-record-dir` 相当) の関係が再び揺れる可能性がある。
- **キーとなる指摘**: 「経路ごとに規則を書くと収束しない」——`-install-wrapper` など複数の経路にパスの規則を別々に実装したところ、レビュー指摘が同じ型で 4 巡続けて再発した。規則は「フラグを読んだ直後の 1 か所」で当て、経路には解決済みの絶対パスだけを渡す構成に直した。**もう一つ、このドキュメント自身が「正本は複製しない」を実践している** — サポートする配置の一覧を `triagecheck/README.md` に一元化し、ここでは言い直さないと明記している。これは work-context の「正本 (single source of truth) discipline」「散文が図を言い直さない」と同じ原則。
- **Severity**: high

#### 2. LLM が組み立てる入力は型で縛る
- **ファイル**: `docs/solutions/design-patterns/typed-contract-for-agent-input.md`（2026-08-01）
- **モジュール**: pr-teeth（別プラグインだが原則は移植可能）
- **Problem Type**: `design_pattern`
- **関連性**: 計画は「記録 YAML as the only hand-off」を維持しつつスキーマを変更する。この学びは、LLM/サブエージェントが組み立てて渡すペイロードに対し `.get()` 的な寛容な読み取りをすると、キー名の取り違えが exit=0・警告なしで握りつぶされることを実例で示している。
- **キーとなる指摘**: 必須性は「検査」ではなく「構造」にする（必須フィールドは位置引数にする、未知キーはエラーにする、falsy だが有効な値 (`0` 等) を欠落と誤判定しない）。記録 YAML に新しいフィールド（プランナー選択、段階ごとの model/effort など）を足す際、Go 側の構造体だけでなく、記録を書き込むスキル側のプロースにも同じ考え方を適用する価値がある。
- **Severity**: high

#### 3. データ種別ごとに失敗時の態度を変える
- **ファイル**: `docs/solutions/architecture-patterns/fail-soft-by-data-class.md`（2026-08-01）
- **モジュール**: pr-teeth
- **Problem Type**: `architecture_pattern`
- **関連性**: 計画は「設定」（`loop.max_rounds` のデフォルト変更、新設定キーの追加）と「記録 YAML」（蓄積・引き継ぎデータ）の両方を同時に変更する。この学びは両者を同じロード関数・同じ既定値フォールバックで扱うと性質の異なる 3 種の不具合が同じ根から生まれると述べている。
- **キーとなる指摘**: 設定は「既定値で続行 + 警告」でよいが、記録（蓄積データ／エージェント入力）は「壊れていれば保存を拒否して停止」が原則。新しい `loop.max_rounds` や planner 選択の設定キーはこれまで通り fail-soft でよいが、記録 YAML のスキーマ変更・書き込みには同じ寛容さを適用しない、という切り分けを計画の実装方針に明記する価値がある。
- **Severity**: high

#### 4. 識別子の抽出は LLM ではなくコードに置く
- **ファイル**: `docs/solutions/design-patterns/extract-identifiers-in-code-not-llm.md`（2026-08-02）
- **モジュール**: pr-teeth
- **Problem Type**: `design_pattern`
- **関連性**: 判断基準は「取り違えた結果を、出力だけ見て誤りと判別できるか」。work-context の「実効モデル」「effort の受け渡し」は、まさにこの基準に当てはまりうる——サブエージェントに渡すモデル名や effort の値を、スキルのプロース内で LLM がその場で解釈・整形すると、取り違えが「それらしく完成したサブエージェント呼び出し」として現れ、レビューでも気づかれない可能性がある。
- **キーとなる指摘**: 「識別子を確定させる場所を 1 箇所に絞る」「同一性の次元を数え上げる」。段階 (調査/立案/修正) ごとに model/effort を受け渡す実装では、その解決ロジックを一箇所のコード（またはテスト済みの決定的な処理）に閉じ込め、スキルのプロースには任せない設計を検討すべき。
- **Severity**: high

### 計画の決定事項と突き合わせて見つけた懸念（学び以外の一次情報）

`recurrence-detection.md` と `reframing.md` を削除する決定について、リポジトリ全体を実際にグレップしたところ、この 2 ファイルを参照している文書が **CONCEPTS.md を含めて 13 件**見つかった（`grep -rl "recurrence-detection\.md\|reframing\.md" --include='*.md' .` の実測）。代表的なもの:
- `CONCEPTS.md` の「修正由来の指摘」節が、両ファイルを名指しで正本として参照している（例: 「条件と例外の正本は `review-triage` の `recurrence-detection.md` で、ここでは言い直さない」）
- `review-triage/skills/review-triage/SKILL.md`, `review-triage/skills/review-triage-fix/SKILL.md`, `review-triage/skills/review-triage-fix/references/grouping.md`, `same-location-fix.md`, `review-triage/skills/review-triage-loop/references/loop-flow.md`, `review-triage/README.md`, `review-triage/skills/review-triage/references/record-schema.md` など

これは学び #1 が述べる「正本を複製しない／複製すると片方だけ更新される型を作り込む」の裏返しで、**正本を消すときは、それを指す全参照側も同時に直す必要がある**ことを実例で裏付けている。計画のタスク分解に「両ファイルへの参照の網羅的な置き換え（CONCEPTS.md を含む）」を明示的な作業項目として入れることを推奨する。

### 隣接する学び（参考、適用は限定的）

- `docs/solutions/tooling-decisions/avoid-dual-parser-implementations.md`（2026-08-01, `tooling_decision`）— 依存回避のための二重実装を避ける、という原則。確認したところ `review-triage/tools/triagecheck/record.go` は既に `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` の単一ライブラリで記録 YAML を読んでおり（自前パーサは無い）、現状はこの失敗パターンに該当しない。ただし記録スキーマに新フィールド（プランナー種別、段階ごとの model/effort）を足す際、シェルラッパーや別スクリプト側で正規表現による簡易パースを新設しないよう注意する価値はある。
- `docs/solutions/conventions/plugin-cannot-resolve-its-own-source.md`（2026-08-01, `convention`）— プラグインは自分の配布元を実行時に知れない、という制約。「effort-variant agent definitions をプラグインに同梱する」という決定に直接関わるものではないが、プラグインの展開先 (CONCEPTS.md の「展開先」) からエージェント定義ファイルを解決するコードを書く場合は、この制約（配布元ごとの設定置き場を推測せずリテラルに持たせる）を思い出す価値がある。

### 推奨事項
1. 記録 YAML のスキーマ変更は、学び #2・#3 に沿って「未知キーは拒否」「必須フィールドの欠落は構造的に検出」「記録の破損時は fail-loud」の方針を実装レベルの受け入れ基準に落とす。
2. サブエージェントへの model/effort の受け渡しは、学び #4 に沿って解決ロジックを一箇所に閉じ込め、決定的な単体テストを付ける。
3. `recurrence-detection.md` / `reframing.md` 削除に伴う 13 件の参照先（`CONCEPTS.md` を含む）の洗い出しと更新を、計画のタスクとして明示する。
4. サブエージェント実行時のカレントディレクトリ・記録の置き場の関係が変わる場合は、学び #1 の「経路ごとに規則を書くと収束しない」を踏まえ、パス解決を 1 か所に集約する設計にする。</result>

(2) How are plugin subagents named/referenced (e.g. `plugin-name:agent-name`)? (3) Can a subagent call AskUserQuestion / ask the user a question? Quote. (4) What does the doc say about permission prompts from a foreground subagent — are they forwarded to the user? (5) Anything about non-interactive `claude -p` and subagents (does the parent wait)? result.output:
# Answers

**(1) Which frontmatter fields are NOT supported / ignored for plugin subagents?**

"For security reasons, plugin subagents don't support the `hooks`, `mcpServers`, or `permissionMode` frontmatter fields. These fields are ignored when loading agents from a plugin."

**(2) How are plugin subagents named/referenced?**

Plugin subagents use a scoped identifier format: `plugin-name:agent-name`. If a plugin organizes agents into subfolders, the path is included: `plugin-name:subfolder:agent-name`. For example, a plugin called `my-plugin` with an agent at `agents/review/security.md` registers as `my-plugin:review:security`.

**(3) Can a subagent call AskUserQuestion / ask the user a question?**

No. The `AskUserQuestion` tool is removed from every subagent: "The first filter removes these tools, even when listed in the `tools` field: ... `AskUserQuestion`"

**(4) What does the doc say about permission prompts from a foreground subagent — are they forwarded to the user?**

Yes, permission prompts are forwarded: "**Foreground subagents** block the main conversation until complete. Permission prompts are passed through to you as they come up."

**(5) Anything about non-interactive `claude -p` and subagents (does the parent wait)?**

Yes. In non-interactive mode with `-p`, fork mode is off: "Fork mode is off in [non-interactive mode](/docs/en/headless) with `-p` and in the Agent SDK unless you turn it on." When fork mode is off and a subagent is not a fork, "Claude runs the subagent in the background by default and in the foreground when it needs the result before continuing." Additionally: "In [non-interactive mode](/docs/en/headless) and the Agent SDK, the launching subagent doesn't wait, so a nested background subagent that finishes after its launcher has ended reports to your main conversation instead."

**(6) What happens when the per-call `model` alias is not permitted/available?**

"Claude Code checks the per-invocation parameter, frontmatter, and environment variable values against your organization's [`availableModels`](/docs/en/model-config#restrict-model-selection) allowlist. For a blocked value, it substitutes another model: When the blocked value is a family alias such as `opus`, Claude Code runs the subagent on the newest version of that family the allowlist permits... For any other blocked value, on providers where that substitution doesn't operate, or when the allowlist permits no version of the family, Claude Code runs the subagent on the inherited model instead."

**(7) Do subagents load CLAUDE.md files? Quote.**

Yes, with exceptions: "A non-fork subagent's initial context contains: ... **CLAUDE.md files**: every level of the [CLAUDE.md hierarchy](/docs/en/memory#how-claude-md-files-load) the main conversation loads, including `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, project rules, `CLAUDE.local.md`, and managed policy files. The built-in Explore and Plan agents skip this. A subagent whose definition sets [`omitClaudeMd`](#supported-frontmatter-fields) loads only the managed policy files, or none at all when the definition comes from [managed settings](#choose-the-subagent-scope)."

研究が 4 つともそろいました。要点を統合すると、要求仕様に書いていない**計画固有の決めどころが 3 つ**出ています (段 1 の結果の置き場・人間の答えの反映経路・旧記録の扱い)。以下、書く前の確認です。

要求仕様は、検知と俯瞰を廃止して繰り返しへの対応を「記録の回 N を越えたら毎回、人間が立案者を選ぶ」形に置き換え、`review-triage-fix` を 3 段にして段ごとに sub-agent で走らせられるようにする、という範囲でした。

この計画は要求仕様の全範囲を扱い、3 つの段階に分けます — (1) 検知・俯瞰の廃止と上限 10、(2) 閾値 N と立案者の選択、(3) 段の sub-agent 化。(1) だけでも出せる順序にします。触るのは 3 つのスキルの手順書と参照文書、記録の様式、周回の状態機械、検査ツール (Go) とそのテスト、README と用語集。新設は agent 定義 6 つと、段の sub-agent の依頼文・検証の参照文書、`review-triage-fix` の引数の参照文書。テストは、検査ツールの変更 (旧様式の受け入れ・新しい状態) に Go のテストを書き、スキルの手順書は記録の fixture で手動の通し確認 (セッション内と sub-agent の両方)、変更した文書には `doc-dag` を回し、廃止した文書への参照が残っていないことを grep で確かめます。採否の判定フローとレビューの起動経路には触りません。

**Carrying forward:**
- 検知の判断をやめ、合図は回数だけ — user-directed (「記録に残すだけ」「閾値で遅らせる」より)
- 俯瞰と捉え直しの廃止 — user-approved
- N は記録の回番号で数える — user-approved
- 回 N+1 以降は毎回止まり人間が A/B/C を選ぶ。設定で既定を持たない — user-directed
- 設計・仕様変更を含む案だけ人間に返す — user-approved
- effort ごとの汎用 agent 定義 6 つ、段は依頼文、model は呼び出し時 — user-approved
- 段の既定はセッション内、sub-agent は段ごとに設定 — user-approved

**Call outs:**
- 段 1 (調査) の結果を置く場所が現行の記録の様式に無い (計画は `approach` が必須) ので、計画の状態に「調査済み・未立案」を 1 つ足す — 「受け渡しは記録だけ」がこれで初めて成立する
- C (人間が立案) の待ちは、新しい状態や周回のノードを足さず、既存の「選択待ち」で表す
- 人間の答え (選択待ちの承認・C の案) を `review-triage-fix` が記録に書いて段 3 から続ける経路と、周回の入口で未着手をレビューより先に片付ける順序を、要求として足す — 現行は「選択待ちは報告だけ」で反映の経路が無く、再起動するとレビューが先に走って直していない問題が再指摘される
- 既存の記録に残る検知の項目は、読み込みと生成サマリの描画を残して整合検査だけ外す — 検査ツールは置き場の全記録を検査するので、未知のキーとして弾くと全ブランチの関門が止まる
- このブランチの最新コミットで入った「同じ場所を再び直す」手順は、発火条件が検知の根拠に依存しているので、記録の指摘の位置だけで判断する形に書き換える
- 段の実行情報 (model・effort) は報告だけで記録には残さず、sub-agent 起動前に記録の写しも取らない — 記録はブランチ単位で短命、壊れたら止めて人間が直す

これで良ければ、要求仕様と研究とこの要約をもとに実装計画を書きます。直したいところがあれば教えてください。
「このブランチの最新コミットで入った「同じ場所を再び直す」手順は、発火条件が検知の根拠に依存している」そのつもりはなかったので、詳しく説明してください

失うのは手順の中身だけです。具体的には次の 3 つで、他の文書には (部分的にしか) ありません。

1. **「数を書かない」** — 列挙の件数を文に書かない規則と、数が要るかの判定基準 (その数を 1 つ増減しても文の主張が変わるか)。`review-triage` の「規範文書に実測値を書かない」は記録から数える値が対象で、規範の中の列挙を数えた値は扱っていません。
2. **「重複を参照にする」** — 修正そのものとして `doc-dag` を使って正本を決め、片方を参照に置き換える手。手順 10 の `doc-dag` は修正の後の確認であって、修正の手ではありません。「範囲で参照する文も複製である」という気づき (「手順 1〜4 と同じ規則」のような文) もここにしかありません。
3. **書き直す前に形を見る、という順序** — 中身を直す前に、その記述が別の記述から導かれる形になっていないかを見ること。

了解しました。「同じ場所」の枠を外し、手 (数を書かない・重複を参照にする・書く前に形を見る) を文書の記述を直すときの常の規則として残します。ファイル名と冒頭はその形に書き換え、git blame や記録の突き合わせは不要になります。

改めた要約です (変わったのは呼び出しの 5 つ目だけ)。

要求仕様は、検知と俯瞰を廃止して繰り返しへの対応を「記録の回 N を越えたら毎回、人間が立案者を選ぶ」形に置き換え、`review-triage-fix` を 3 段にして段ごとに sub-agent で走らせられるようにする、という範囲でした。

この計画は要求仕様の全範囲を扱い、3 つの段階に分けます — (1) 検知・俯瞰の廃止と上限 10、(2) 閾値 N と立案者の選択、(3) 段の sub-agent 化。(1) だけでも出せる順序にします。触るのは 3 つのスキルの手順書と参照文書、記録の様式、周回の状態機械、検査ツール (Go) とそのテスト、README と用語集。新設は agent 定義 6 つと、段の sub-agent の依頼文・検証の参照文書、`review-triage-fix` の引数の参照文書。テストは、検査ツールの変更 (旧様式の受け入れ・新しい状態) に Go のテストを書き、スキルの手順書は記録の fixture で手動の通し確認 (セッション内と sub-agent の両方)、変更した文書には `doc-dag` を回し、廃止した文書への参照が残っていないことを grep で確かめます。採否の判定フローとレビューの起動経路には触りません。

**Carrying forward:**
- 検知の判断をやめ、合図は回数だけ — user-directed
- 俯瞰と捉え直しの廃止 — user-approved
- N は記録の回番号で数える — user-approved
- 回 N+1 以降は毎回止まり人間が A/B/C を選ぶ。設定で既定を持たない — user-directed
- 設計・仕様変更を含む案だけ人間に返す — user-approved
- effort ごとの汎用 agent 定義 6 つ、段は依頼文、model は呼び出し時 — user-approved
- 段の既定はセッション内、sub-agent は段ごとに設定 — user-approved
- 「同じ場所を再び直す」は手だけ残して枠を外す — user-approved (「削除」「検知から切り離して残す」より)

**Call outs:**
- 段 1 (調査) の結果を置く場所が現行の記録の様式に無いので、計画の状態に「調査済み・未立案」を 1 つ足す — 「受け渡しは記録だけ」がこれで初めて成立する
- C (人間が立案) の待ちは、新しい状態や周回のノードを足さず、既存の「選択待ち」で表す
- 人間の答え (選択待ちの承認・C の案) を `review-triage-fix` が記録に書いて段 3 から続ける経路と、周回の入口で未着手をレビューより先に片付ける順序を、要求として足す — 現行は反映の経路が無く、再起動するとレビューが先に走って直していない問題が再指摘される
- 既存の記録に残る検知の項目は、読み込みと生成サマリの描画を残して整合検査だけ外す — 未知のキーとして弾くと全ブランチの関門が止まる
- 段の実行情報 (model・effort) は報告だけで記録には残さず、sub-agent 起動前に記録の写しも取らない — 記録はブランチ単位で短命、壊れたら止めて人間が直す

これで良ければ、要求仕様と研究とこの要約をもとに実装計画を書きます。直したいところがあれば教えてください。
